I'm not a sailor, but I seem to recall that about 7 miles away from you a ship will appear to sink, not disappear. That observation of the curve of the earth affecting your sighting of the ship is called "hull down" and was good enough for Columbus.

I got a cheap round the world airline ticket in 1989 and again in 1991. I went west from NYC and if I took a detour in any other direction I had to pay extra, which I did to get to Nepal. Once I wangled a free ticket going east from NYC, but I didn't make many stops, just Zurich, Bangkok and back to NYC. I wish Terry Pratchett's Disc World was real, but I didn't see it. 

Why would governments, explorers, and scientists world wide for centuries try to hide that the earth is flat?
Asking about motivation often puts paid to the wilder conspiracy stories.

comments.name: Tstarwich

Thank you for this thoughtful article. As a holistic health coach and a 66-year-old woman, I often wonder what I would tell my 50-year-old self. I would tell her to worry less about being thin and focus more on nourishing her body with calcium-rich foods, adequate protein, strength-building movement, and healthy lifestyle habits.

But most importantly, I would encourage her to make an emotional shift in how she views aging.

The woman in this article who still holds on to clothes from 30 years ago really struck me. How many of us are doing the same thing, physically or emotionally? Holding on to an image of ourselves that no longer reflects who we are becoming?

Many women of my generation were raised to believe that thinness equaled beauty, desirability, and even self-worth. We have spent decades trying to control our weight, often at the expense of appreciating our bodies.

Of course, excess weight can carry health risks, but a few extra pounds as we age do not necessarily mean we are unhealthy. Perhaps it's time to shift our attention away from trying to reclaim our younger bodies and toward building strength, nourishing ourselves, and embracing the natural changes of aging.

I believe healthy aging is as much an emotional and spiritual transition as it is a physical one. What if we spent less energy trying to look like the women we were at 30 and more energy appreciating the women we are becoming?

comments.name: Kt
comments.body: I'm 64yrs old and began heavy lifting at 18 yrs old as a member of a College Varsity Crew team. I've been an athlete my entire life, a team every season, Crew through college, running and lifting ever since. I needed to stop running this past year due to spinal issues, and in my early 40's I suffered through about 12 years of heavy prednisone usage with antibiotics due to an immunodeficiency that took too long to diagnose. As a woman, I've been on a lifetime diet--but when I was really sick with infections, I dropped to 122lbs at 5'8"--too thin. I regained weight and held steady at 128lb, lifting through all the illness when I could. After menopause and weekly immunoglobulin infusions, I'm now arbout 136lbs at 5'7". Would I like to be a bit thinner--yes, but I was shocked when my last bone scan revealed osteopenia--despite teaching two weight classes a week (group instructor and Personal Trainer), heavy lifting on my own afterwards in addition to a 3rd time a week. BMI should NOT be used--it can not account for muscle weight--other measurements must be used to accurately assess a person's healthy weight. Overall, so thankful for this article as I've seen too many women postmenopausal on GLP-1s, thrilled to have lost weight, but risking major bone loss as they wrongly lift very light weights so as 'not to bulk up'!

comments.name: New Englander
comments.body: Did the study referenced in the article control for low weight associated with underlying medical conditions? If some of the study participants had low weight associated with disease or life-style choices (nutrition, alcohol consumption), then the findings would be flawed. Further, did the investigators look at an association between weight and mortality at different older ages? Were the results the same at 70, 80, 90 for example? How about differences among participants of different socioeconomic or racial groups? Was quality of diet factored in? It is a complicated hypothesis that needs a large study incorporating many controls. If the study did not control for these and other factors, then the  conclusion that older people benefit from additional weight was not demonstrated.

The forty senators from the twenty least populated states represent 11% of the U.S. population, but can stymie the intent of the other 89% of the U.S. population.

On the other hand the fifty senators from the twenty five least populated states represent 16% of the U.S. population and can theoretically pass a bill that's opposed by 84% of the people, though such a bill would be unlikely to pass in the House.

 To refer to this system as a democracy is obviously ridiculous.

Because it cannot be guaranteed that radicals will always be denied power, the filibuster may prove necessary from time to time, but should only delay a vote on a bill if the forty + one senators voting against cloture represent at least 40% of the U.S. population rather than the 11% currently required. comments.name: Paul Mow
comments.body:
I think you have it wrong here. The fiancée’s has an interest in knowing the truth, but the Ethicist overlooks the ethical responsibility of the person conveying the information.

There are two separate ethical questions here:
* Does the fiancée deserve to know? If true, probably yes. She should have an opportunity to make an informed decision before marrying.
* Who should tell her? That’s where I disagree with the Ethicist.

The woman in the relationship has firsthand knowledge. She can explain what happened, when it happened, and what she knew about the man’s relationship status. She may also have text messages or other evidence supporting her account.

The letter writer, by contrast, has no personal knowledge of the alleged infidelity. He/She would be repeating someone else’s account to a woman he/she barely knows.

That’s hearsay even if the information happens to be true. And while hearsay isn’t necessarily false, it carries obvious risks of misunderstanding, misinterpretation, exaggeration, incomplete context, and possibly later denial by the source of its accuracy.

There’s another problem: The Ethicist effectively allows the person with firsthand knowledge to avoid the uncomfortable consequences of disclosure while encouraging a third party to assume that burden. That strikes me as ethically inconsistent.

If the friend believes strongly enough that the fiancée deserves to know, she should be willing to take responsibility for communicating what she personally knows.

As they say, nothing good lasts forever. Said executive was known for a dictatorial style, intolerance for dissent, and never wanted to hear bad news. Various problems, particularly with manufacturing, festered unseen by shareholders and customers alike. When things got so bad regulators shut down manufacturing, and my company was referring customers to our competitors' products, time was up. Soon he was out, the company was bought for a fraction of what it should have been, and now there's no trace of it. There simply is no substitute for good corporate governance. An ineffectual board is a recipe for eventual disaster. It's just a matter of time. I tend to think having anyone from the C-suite on the board should be outawed.

comments.name: Mariallivia

Publicly traded companies have a fudiciary responsibility, which is a legal obligation requiring the board of directors to act in the best financial intersts of the corporation and its shareholders:

 Duty of Loyalty: Executives and board members must put the company’s interests above their own personal, financial, or romantic interests. Engaging in undisclosed relationships with business counterparties (like Alice Huang at Megaspeed) or subordinates creates severe conflicts of interest, exposes the company to blackmail or regulatory penalties, and violates this duty. 

Duty of Care: Leaders must make informed, prudent decisions and maintain reasonable oversight to protect company assets and value. When a CEO's personal conduct triggers federal investigations, national security scrutiny, or reputational damage that threatens shareholder value, the board of directors has a fiduciary duty to investigate and, if necessary, remove the executive to protect the company.

We are a species that has evolved in a dynamic, ever-changing and unpredictable natural world. Chaos, and adapting to said chaos underpins everything.

Our cognitive, emotional and physical well being are interconnected --all parts completing the system that is the human body. 

Study after study confirms the central importance of exercise. Is exercise alone a panacea? Unfortunately, no. But does being physically (and intellectually) active make this brief spin around the sun more tolerable and sometimes joyous? Absolutely.

Oh, to once again have the morning newspaper thrown onto the porch by the passing boy riding his bicycle. 
Sometimes he would miss, and then our morning started with a quick search through the nearby shrubs. 
But on the mornings when his aim was true, the folded newspaper would land with a thunk, and it is that thunk that I remember most clearly. 
More than the shrilling alarm clock or the heavenly aroma of coffee a-brewing, the thunk was our reliable morning call to start the day....our reveille.

A longtime fan of yours, I was inspired by reading Rock Springs to become a writer myself. You graciously invited me to have a coffee and discuss writing with me. You told me it was your birthday, and I wondered what you were doing alone in Chicago on your big day? And I wondered later, if it really WAS your bday, but never bothered or wanted to fact check because, regardless, I had gotten to I spend a few minutes with one of my favorite scribes. You told me Wildfire was your favorite book of all you had written at that time (1998). I read it immediately, and so glad I did. The word “obsidian” makes me think of you and wildfires. And, I have found the unknowability of people, even those we think we are closest to is, infinite. Happy birthday and many more.

comments.name: Carl Ian Schwartz

Mr. Ford, this is an absolutely beautiful essay, and drives home much of what's missing in today's world and breadth, depth, and factual content of what people are reading (or listening to or watching on podcasts, which I feel take more time and tell too little than well-written words).

Born in July 1951, I am very much my parents' child. However, both coming of age towards the end of the Depression and both civilian employees of the U.S. Army Signal Corps (how they met in late 1943 over a telephone call), they raised me as a child of the 1940s. 

The events you cite from your birth date's Times are events I learned orally from my parents, in classrooms and textbooks, in independent reading, and from the excellent, fact-based documentaries required of our broadcasting networks.

Where I differ from you is the value of coincidences. As my life winds down and my time past exceeds expectations of the future, I DO look at the coincidences in my life as I sum things up at 75. Tears of mourning of those I lost have become tears of remembrance and gratitude for having known them and by that time together we have formed each others' characters. 

"Six Degrees of Separation" is not simply a play or the movie made from it. It's a fact, and a fact we should all live by as we share this planet and try to ensure its future.

You were talking about a review of your first novel and how I think you said it was a critic from The New York Times, criticized it. comments.body: There might be a handful of people in NYC who fully understand and have experience with the geotechnical, underpinning, and lateral support demands of sensitive construction work around older buildings . Such considerations can be seen as gratuitously esoteric and burdensome (expensive hand digging and tunneling work by skilled tradesmen might be needed to deal with these intersecting issues). Arcane, critical path busting time demands are tempting to shortcut,. Well-credentialed professionals may claim to have a command of these issues. But it helps to have both engineering degrees plus time being in the muck capping or replacing decayed underpinning piles by hand. It’s difficult stuff to contend with. Expensive or not, safety should come first.

comments.name: Maureen Entera
comments.body:
I spent yesterday morning  walking along Santa Barbara's Shoreline bluffs and looking down at the swell that had obliterated the sand beaches, and pounded the cliffs holding us up. Sea Level rise has already eroded so much of the cliffs that we lost about ten feet of it in the past two years. 

At this rate, the multi-million dollar homes along the top of the bluffs will be beachfront properties in ten years, and not in a good way.

A most intrepid explorer going where no one has gone before and where few believed he could. Cue Star Trek a cappella theme. Wa wa, wa wa wa wa wa…

comments.name: peter mattsson
comments.body:
As quoted towards the end of the article, Fort Point is the spot right under the Golden Gate Bridge, and not 3 miles west. Less than a mile to the west is Deadman's, and that is a dangerous but fun left. Fort Point is also a left. Fort Cronkite is across the GG Bridge, three miles to the west - maybe that's the correct reference? And Cronkite is difficult on bid days, but usually a small wave spot, slower waves than OB due to nature of the beach. I say this since I surfed and lived near Ocean Beach in San Francisco for 20 years, and surfed every break, small days to easy double overhead at OB. Good times, but OB is dangerous on big days, and an awfully hard paddle out - and somedays even the best surfer can't make it out in spite of best efforts. Sometimes OB willl let you out, sometimes she won't - all hail Mother Nature :)
Thank you for the great coverage - I'm now in Charlottesville, Va...and get to surf Ocracoke Island, Hatteras, or the Atlantic Wave Pool in Virginia Beach. Good times, but I miss NorCal - surf, snow, sailing! Enjoy the west for this Cville Fella!!

comments.name: Jennu
comments.body: More or less flat here on the East Coast.  Today it would be a long drive to the OBX for some waist high chop.  My idea of good waves is a little overhead; more than that gets hard to deal with.   On Surfline Mavericks is blown out, but Ventura Point looks entirely worthwhile, and crowded.  I’ll go to the pool and mow the lawn instead.

comments.name: Ilovecomments
comments.body: I was on West Cliff in Santa Cruz yesterday and saw not just the street, cars & onlookers get swamped, but the houses across the street got a saltwater shower too. I've lived here for almost 40 years and have only seen waves like that one other time. No surfers in the water- the ocean was a washing machine and looked very dangerous.

You already know "their" card.  Don't forget it!  Split deck into 3 piles--from the bottom, about 10 each. Keep, say, 20 cards.  Next turnover the top 3 cards from the 20 in your hand, lay them face up, one on each of the 3 piles.  You then instruct your "mark" to privately, look at the top card (the 4th which you already know) and to mix it into the pile of 20 cards that was in your hand.  Meanwhile you focus on the 3 piles--all a diversion.  You do some fake math--one ruse is to start with the turned over card and use the cards underneath it to count to 10.  If it's a 3 you'll need 7 cards, an 8, 2, a face card none.  Count out loud...say "hmmm....ok"  Then ask for the deck with the 4th card now shuffled into.  Now for the big ta da and killer ruse.  Start turning over the cards.  GO PAST his/her (the 4th card) by a few, depending where it is....better to go aways past it.  Then with a few cards still face down in your hand boast:  "How much (do you wanna bet?) the next card I turn over is your card?"  Your mark will be salivating thinking victory is nigh and bet the moon.  You accept, hover backwards--do this slowly, they will start to despair and  turnover the already turned over 4th card upside down.  Boom! "The building that collapsed had a litany of unresolved violations: exposed electrical wiring, missing smoke detectors and an inadequate water supply for the sprinkler system,"
